Rancor

RANG-ker · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Rancor is longstanding and bitter resentment.

The rancor between the two rival chefs went back to a cooking competition neither of them would ever discuss.

Worked Example

Thirty years after the merger that cost him his company, the old founder still spoke of his former partner with undisguised rancor, refusing to even say the man's name.

Rancor is deep, long-lasting bitterness -- decades haven't softened the founder's resentment at all.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bitterness: Bitterness is the sour, lasting hurt a person carries after a disappointment or injury. Rancor is bitterness at its most entrenched: longstanding, aimed at a particular person, and still sharp years later. Ordinary bitterness can slowly fade; rancor has settled in and hardened.

resentment: Resentment is bitter indignation at being treated unfairly, and it can be quite recent -- you can resent yesterday's snub. Rancor is what resentment becomes when it festers: an old, deep, personal grudge that years have not softened.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

goodwill: friendly, helpful feelings toward others

harmony: a state of agreement and peaceful relations

Where it sits · how deep the bitterness runs — displeasure → rancor → hatred

displeasure vs. rancor: Displeasure is far milder than rancor -- a passing flicker of dissatisfaction that fades on its own, nothing like the bitterness rancor carries for years.

hatred vs. rancor: Hatred is an intense, often more general ill will -- even stronger than the deep, specific bitterness of rancor.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — ranc-

root — ranc-: to be rank, to stink, to go bad (Latin rancere)

suffix — -or

suffix — -or: a state or condition (noun-forming) (Latin -or)

Put it together

Put it together: Rancor comes from Latin rancere ('to be rank, to go bad') + -or -- the idea of a feeling that has 'gone rancid' through prolonged bitterness.

Use the root in a new word: rancid

Use the root in a new word: rancid: The butter had gone rancid after sitting out in the summer heat for a week.

Root Check

Word Choice

Rancor names the deep, lingering bitterness itself -- a feeling that can persist for years -- which sets it apart from umbrage (a more immediate feeling of being offended by one specific remark) and from invective (the abusive language someone might use to express that bitterness out loud).
